heading: Government Advertising Bill (Bills) - 29/10/2026
subject: Government Advertising Bill
parts: The Hon. R.A. Simms interjecting:

The Hon. R.P. WORTLEY: You often refer to him as the grim reaper. He is not doing it. But the bad news is I am. So I rise to indicate that the government will oppose the Government Advertising Bill 2026. The government's position is that the bill largely duplicates safeguards already in place. This includes mandatory advertising guidelines, restrictions on political advertising, established approval processes and the Auditor-General's power to scrutinise government advertising expenditure.

All state government marketing communications must already comply with the publicly available marketing communications guidelines. Those guidelines prohibit the use of public funds for paid advertising that could be interpreted as political, including advertising featuring a politician's voice or image. There is also an existing framework for independent scrutiny. Under the Public Finance and Audit Act 1987, the Auditor-General already has the authority to audit government advertising and report directly to parliament on matters of public interest. The audit provisions proposed in this bill overlap with those existing powers.

The bill would also require advertising expenditure exceeding $10,000 during an election period to be approved by the Auditor-General or authorised by both houses of parliament. In considering that proposal, members should recognise that an approval process is already in place. Since 1 November 2022, all paid government communications and marketing initiatives have been subject to the government communications approval process.

Beyond this duplication, the government is concerned about the proposed prohibition on advertising relating to legislation before parliament. Such a restriction could limit legitimate public consultation and reduce opportunities for the community to participate in the legislative process. Finally, the bill would require a dedicated report on the delivery of election commitments. The government's position is that this information is already made publicly available through regular media releases and announcements as milestones are achieved.

heading: Government Advertising Bill (Bills) - 29/10/2026
subject: Government Advertising Bill
parts: Section 6 would prohibit government advertising that refers to bills or amendments currently under debate. This provision is also important. Public advertising should not be used to influence debate on legislation while that legislation is being considered by parliament. The parliamentary process must be respected and the use of public funds to promote a government's position during legislative debates raises legitimate concerns about fairness and accountability.

Sections 7 and 8 provide for the Auditor-General to assess potential breaches of these provisions and establish the reporting processes where a breach has occurred. Giving the Auditor-General a role in overseeing compliance is an important feature of this bill. Effective rules are only meaningful if there is an independent mechanism—a truly independent mechanism—that assesses whether they have been followed and to report any breaches to parliament.

Part 4 addresses advertising expenditure in the lead-up to an election. Under this part, agencies would be restricted to spending a total of $10,000 on advertising during a period from 1 July in the year before an election and ending on election day, unless approval is granted by the Auditor-General or through a resolution passed by both houses of parliament. The Auditor-General can only approve expenditure where satisfied that the advertising is necessary for the proper function of government, with details of approvals required to be published monthly. This provision seeks to address a fundamental concern: the potential for governments to use the resources of the state to their electoral advantage.

An incumbent government has considerable advantages. It has access to public resources, government communication channels and the machinery of government itself. There must be appropriate safeguards to ensure those resources are not used to give any political party an unfair political advantage in the lead-up to an election.

heading: Government Advertising Bill (Bills) - 29/10/2026
subject: Government Advertising Bill
parts: All this is happening during a cost-of-living crisis, when South Australian families are struggling to pay their mortgages, electricity bills and grocery bills. Apparently, there is always money available when it comes to political parties and government advertising. Let me be clear: I recognise that governments need to communicate important public information, particularly around health, safety and emergencies, but there is a fundamental difference between informing the public and promoting the government.

Taxpayers should not be paying for political self-congratulation. That is why I support this bill's proposed restrictions on government advertising, particularly the requirement for independent approval of expenditure exceeding $10,000 during the specified pre-election period. The Auditor-General's oversight is an important safeguard against the misuse of public funds for political advantage. I supported the 2024 electoral reforms because I believe greater accountability and integrity are important for our democracy, but integrity cannot stop at political donations. It must also apply to how government spends taxpayer money.

If we are going to ask South Australians to fund our democratic system, then we have an even greater obligation to ensure their money is not used to give the government of the day an unfair political advantage. At a time when every dollar matters to South Australian households, surely the same standard should apply to the government. Public money should be spent serving the public, not securing the political future of those in power. I commend the Hon. Robert Simms for bringing this bill forward, and I support the bill.

heading: Road Maintenance (Motions) - 28/10/2026
subject: Road Maintenance
parts: In fact, every day families rely on safe roads to get their kids to school, workers rely on them to get to work, ambulances rely on them to reach people who need help and regional families rely on them to get to sport, medical appointments and essential services. It should go without saying that safe and reliable roads are not a luxury. They are the bare minimum that South Australians should be able to expect from their state government, yet our road network is deteriorating, and the backlog is growing.

South Australia has approximately 13,000 kilometres of sealed roads and 10,000 kilometres of unsealed roads. The Auditor-General has noted that the Department for Infrastructure and Transport has estimated in 2023 that $2.1 billion was needed to repair roads in very poor condition. The actual maintenance figures tell their own story. In the five years to June 2026, road depreciation totalled $1.8 billion. Over that same period just $884 million was spent on road maintenance. In other words, our road network is wearing out faster than we can maintain it.

That should concern every South Australian, because putting off necessary road maintenance does not make the problem go away; in fact, it only makes it worse and ultimately more expensive. It risks making repairs more expensive for taxpayers down the track, and motorists are already paying the price.

heading: Road Maintenance (Motions) - 28/10/2026

parts: When we came to government, there was a significant backlog, $1.6 billion…and the then Liberal government did make significant inroads.

In fact, as has been well documented by the Auditor-General, when the Liberals came to government in 2018, the maintenance backlog stood at $750 million. When they left office, four years later, it was almost $2 billion. Frankly, it is alarming that someone who styles herself as the alternative Premier of South Australia could be so off the mark. For the benefit of the member for Schubert, that difference is more than $1 billion and occurred in the term of the Marshall Liberal government. heading: Road Maintenance (Motions) - 28/10/2026
subject: Road Maintenance
parts: Four out of five budgets in that period were written by this government. A government that talks up its budget management while running down its road network is not managing anything. It is borrowing from the bitumen and hoping nobody checks the books.

The scale of the problem is not disputed by anyone who drives these roads. South Australia has roughly 13,000 kilometres of sealed and 10,000 kilometres of unsealed state roads. The Auditor-General has reported that the Department for Infrastructure and Transport's own 2023 estimate that $2.1 billion was needed to repair roads in very poor condition, and that has been confirmed, of course, by the RAA as well. In June last year, the RAA found that more than two and a half thousand kilometres of the network was in urgent need of repair. It described cracking, potholes, crumbling shoulders as routine, most especially in the regions.

Let me turn to what this costs the people I speak for as shadow minister for small and family business. I routinely have phone calls with freight operators, with primary producers, calling me and describing the perilous state of our roads down in the South-East, the cost of which gets added onto every load because of suspension going out, the time in the maintenance workshops, the time of those trucks off the road not delivering the freight that our state desperately needs, and it is simply because our roads are not truck worthy. Our roads are not car worthy, even though those freight operators and those driving their kids to school or getting down to the local shops from outside the city bounds of Mount Gambier are required to have their cars roadworthy.

I want to touch on privatisation, because my good friend the Treasurer, the Hon. Tom Koutsantonis, brings this up quite a bit whenever we are on radio together. I always enjoy being on radio with Mr Koutsantonis. If the government really and truly believed outsourcing road maintenance caused this problem, that the contract is a dog, as they have said time and time again, it is had 4½ years to bring the work back inhouse, and it has not done so.

All it has done is keep referring to this contract, and the Auditor-General over the last 4½ years has consistently referred to that contract as saying it has not been managed correctly by the department. It is had 4½ years to sort this stuff out, but the government has chosen not to. It has kept the model that it attacks, kept collecting the political benefit of attacking it and let the network deteriorate in the meantime. If the policy was so bad, members opposite should explain why they have kept it.

This government was elected in March 2022 and re-elected this year. It has framed five budgets. At some point, the government has to accept responsibility for the roads it has been maintaining—or failing to maintain—for almost a decade. Blaming the previous government does not fill a single pothole. None of this is complicated. A competent government budgets for the depreciation of its asset. It maintains the roads before they need rebuilding, because it is cheaper. It treats the regional network as economic infrastructure, not a political afterthought, because that is where the state's exports start their journey, and it does not ask families to choose between a long detour or a road they no longer trust. It does not ask mums and dads when their kids get their Ps to tell their kids, 'I don't want you driving on these roads.' I have done that to my 20-year-old daughter, time and time again.

heading: North Adelaide Golf Course (Motions) - 28/10/2026
subject: North Adelaide Golf Course

I move this motion because the findings of the Auditor-General raise serious questions about the Malinauskas Labor government's handling of taxpayers' money, its procurement practices and, perhaps most concerningly, its unwillingness to be transparent about either. This government seems to have developed a rather casual attitude towards spending other people's money.

When questions are asked about spending that money, the answers are either difficult to come by or simply not forthcoming. Those who do the asking are quickly subjected to an ad hominem attack. Instead of answering these valid questions, the government have quickly developed a predictable routine of attacking those who dare ask rather than addressing the substance of the question. That is not good enough. South Australians have every right to know how their hard-earned taxpayer funds are being spent, particularly when the Auditor-General has identified significant shortcomings in the processes that are supposed to safeguard those dollars.

Let's look at what the Auditor-General has revealed. Fourteen specialist consultants, which we know include high-profile golfer Greg Norman, were engaged to work on the North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment without a competitive procurement process—14 consultants, all initially engaged on contracts valued at $55,000. Conveniently, that meant that many of the usual requirements under the Department of the Premier and Cabinet's procurement policy did not apply.

I am sure the government will tell us that there is nothing to see here, but I would suggest that 14 contracts, all sitting conveniently at a threshold that would otherwise trigger greater scrutiny, deserves a very close look indeed. It gets worse. When those initial contracts expired, the government extended 11 of those contracts. This time, according to the Auditor-General, every one of those contracts was valued at more than more than $55,000. Is that not extraordinary? So, 14 consultants initially were engaged below the threshold of $55,000. Anything above $55,000 has that additional procurement scrutiny. So 14 consultants were engaged so that additional procurements scrutiny did not apply, followed by 11 contract extensions above that very threshold. It is an extraordinary coincidence.

Apparently, some of those contracts subsequently increased significantly in value, yet the department failed to prepare the acquisition plans and purchase recommendations required under its own procurement policy. Let me repeat that: the department responsible for overseeing this government's administration failed to prepare documentation required under its own procurement rules.

This is not simply an allegation made by the opposition. These are findings identified by the independent Auditor-General. The Auditor-General also found that the department had not retained sufficient evidence of its value-for-money assessments for contracts and extensions. In other words, the department could not adequately demonstrate that taxpayers were getting value for the money that was being spent.

Perhaps most damningly, the Auditor-General was unable to conclude whether the department had complied with the procurement requirements during stage 1 of this project because the necessary document had not been provided. Think about that for a moment. The independent officer charged with scrutinising government expenditure could not establish whether the government's own procurement rules had been followed.

If the Auditor-General cannot get a full picture, what hope does the South Australian taxpayer have? We are talking about public money, not the Premier's money, not the Treasurer's money, not the Labor Party's money. It is money earned by South Australians who go to work every day, who pay their taxes and who quite reasonably expect their government to spend those dollars responsibly.

At a time when households are struggling because of cost of living, businesses are under significant financial pressure and, quite frankly, regional communities are crying out for investment in essential infrastructure, the government should be able to account for every dollar it spends. Instead, we have a situation where consultants have been engaged without competitive procurement, contracts have been increased significantly in value, required documentation has not been prepared, and the Auditor-General has been left unable to determine whether the rules were followed. All of this relates to a golf course redevelopment. Greg Norman might be the Shark, but it appears South Australian taxpayers are the ones getting bitten.

I want to make something very clear before I am subjected to an ad hominem attack by the Premier and his government. This motion is not about whether Greg Norman or any other consultant has the expertise to contribute to a golf course redevelopment. It is about the decisions made by this government. Who authorised these contracts? Why were they initially structured at that $55,000 threshold? What justification was provided for the subsequent increases? How much money has ultimately been paid out to each consultant? Who were the 14 consultants? Where is the evidence that these arrangements represented value for money?

It is worth pointing out, I think, that history has shown us that attacks of this nature are often the last refuge of those who cannot mount a credible argument. When the facts are inconvenient and a sound, logical rebuttal is lacking, attacking the individual rather than addressing the substance becomes the preferred tactic. The motion before the chamber requires the government, within three sitting days, to produce all documents relating to consultants and contractor contracts for the redevelopment, including initial contracts, extensions, variations and change requests.

It also, as I pointed out initially, seeks correspondence between DPC and consultants and contractors concerning those negotiations, with internal briefings and correspondence relating to those contracts. These are the documents that will allow this parliament to examine what decisions were made, why they were made, and whether the proper process was followed. This government cannot expect South Australians to simply take its word that everything was above board when its own documentation has been found wanting by the Auditor-General.

There is a very simple principle at stake here. Transparency is not something government should offer only when it is politically convenient. Accountability is not an option, and compliance with procurement rules is not some bureaucratic inconvenience to be brushed aside when a government wants to get a project moving. These rules exist for a reason. They exist to protect public money, to ensure fairness and competition, and to prevent precisely the sort of questions that have now arisen over this redevelopment.

If the Malinauskas Labor government wants South Australians to have confidence in its management of public finances, then it must be prepared to be transparent, not issue another carefully worded media statement, not hide behind departmental processes, and certainly not dismiss legitimate questions about the expenditure of taxpayer funds. Produce those contracts, produce the correspondence and produce the evidence—that is what we are asking for today in this motion.

Members opposite might not like the questions being asked, but that does not absolve them of their responsibility to answer them. If government members choose to oppose this motion, then they will need to explain to South Australians why they believe contracts involving public money should be shielded from parliamentary scrutiny, particularly in the face of the Auditor-General's findings. What is so unreasonable about asking to see the paperwork? What is so difficult about explaining how much consultants were paid and what possible justification there could be for refusing to provide the documents that would establish whether taxpayers receive value for money?

Today, the Premier and the government can put these questions to rest. They can support the motion and undertake to provide these documents, explain the procurement decisions and demonstrate that the public interest was protected—until that happens, serious questions will remain. I urge all honourable members in this chamber to support this motion and I commend it.

heading: Proton Therapy Project (Motions) - 28/10/2026
subject: Proton Therapy Project
parts: I rise today to move for the establishment of a select committee into the Australian Bragg Centre proton therapy project. I want members of this council to imagine being the parent of a child diagnosed with cancer. Imagine being told that a world-class treatment facility was being built right here in Adelaide, offering your child access to advanced cancer treatment without having to travel overseas. That was the promise of the Australian Bragg Centre, a facility expected to treat approximately 700 cancer patients every year, particularly children with certain cancers and adults with rare tumours. But years later, the proton therapy bunker sits empty.

The building was constructed, the commercial agreements were entered into, public money was spent, but the cancer treatment that justified the project has not been delivered. The Auditor-General's June 2025 report revealed that $115.4 million in public funding had been committed to the project: $47.4 million from the state government and $68 million from the commonwealth. Approximately $98.5 million had already been spent and that does not account for the full extent of the state's ongoing leasing commitments and other financial exposures.

What concerns me most is the astronomical financial and commercial risk taken in proceeding with the construction of this facility without first securing a financially viable private operator for the proton therapy unit. How do you commission a purpose-built medical facility costing hundreds of millions of dollars without first securing the commercial arrangements necessary to operate it?

The original building development budget was approximately $372 million, yet the Auditor-General found that the business case relied on assumptions about attracting a private sector operator willing to contribute capital to the project. PwC raised concerns about the lack of evidence supporting that operating model. The Auditor-General subsequently found that the government could not demonstrate that those concerns had been adequately assessed before approving the relevant funding conditions. This raises fundamental questions about the role of SAHMRI and its board.

SAHMRI was responsible for managing the project, including the procurement of the proton therapy equipment and the commercial arrangements supporting the development. I want this inquiry to establish what the SAHMRI board knew, what it approved, and why it proceeded with such extraordinary financial commitments before securing a viable operator. Were board members fully informed of the risks? What independent advice did they receive? What was the contingency plan if the proposed commercial model failed? Who ultimately accepted responsibility for exposing public money to these risks?

This brings me to Commercial & General. Commercial & General financed and developed the Australian Bragg Centre. I want this inquiry to examine how Commercial & General was selected, what procurement process was followed, whether alternative developers were considered, and what role the SAHMRI board played in approving those arrangements. Were there independent commercial assessments? Were potential conflicts of interest identified and appropriately managed? Were the contractual arrangements structured to protect taxpayers if the proton therapy project failed? These are the questions that deserve proper parliamentary scrutiny.

The original leasing arrangements are particularly concerning. The state government committed approximately $91.7 million over 12 years to lease five floors of the Australian Bragg Centre. The Auditor-General reported that this commitment was made to enable the development to achieve financial close. That raises a fundamental question: was the government leasing office accommodation it genuinely needed, or was it taking on a substantial financial commitment to make a commercial development viable? Who determined the rental rates? Were independent valuations and market comparisons undertaken? Did these arrangements represent value for money?

The project also involved a 99-year ground lease, 30-year leasing obligations for SAHMRI and the proton therapy entity, and the government commitments relating to construction cost overruns. Under the development arrangements, the state agreed to meet 70 per cent of certain cost overruns until the building owner's contribution reached its cap and 100 per cent beyond that threshold. These were substantial financial risks.

We must also examine the selection of ProTom International. In 2018, SAHMRI entered into a contract worth approximately $US49.5 million for the proton therapy equipment, yet a 2017 KPMG review had identified significant risks concerning ProTom's financial capacity, demonstrated product success and ability to deliver.

The Auditor-General found no evidence that key information about those risks was communicated to the then Premier. SAHMRI subsequently terminated the contract in October 2024. ABC reporting has revealed that SAHMRI is suing ProTom for approximately $US32 million, alleging misleading and deceptive conduct. ProTom disputes those allegations and maintains that it could still deliver the equipment if the contract were revived. The matter is before the Supreme Court, and I do not intend to prejudge those proceedings, but parliament must still examine why ProTom was selected, what warnings were received and how those risks were managed.

The Auditor-General also identified significant gaps in government oversight. The cross-agency steering committee had not met since late 2021, required project status reports had not been submitted since August 2022, and there was no documented government project management plan. For a project involving this level of public investment, these findings demand serious examination.

Beyond the contracts, the leases and the financial commitments, we must remember the people this project was supposed to help: children fighting cancer and parents desperately searching for treatment options. For them, this was never simply another building on North Terrace. It represented hope, and I find it deeply troubling that substantial financial risks were accepted in a project intended to serve some of our most vulnerable patients. We are talking about taxpayer money, but we are also talking about children's lives and the opportunities for treatments that have been delayed. The consequences of these decisions cannot be measured in dollars alone.

heading: Rural Industry Adjustment and Development (Loan Interest) Amendment Bill (Bills) - 28/10/2026
subject: Rural Industry Adjustment and Development (Loan Interest) Amendment Bill
parts: When the legislation was introduced, there was a clear focus on supporting industries and regions where structural adjustment and redevelopment were required. There was also recognition that producers seeking that adjustment or redevelopment may not always be able to obtain the necessary finance through normal commercial credit sources. Forty-one years later, the principle remains just as relevant.

Today, according to the Auditor-General, approximately $28.4 million remains in the Rural Industry Adjustment and Development Fund. At the same time, parts of South Australia's primary industries are experiencing significant structural pressures. Nowhere is that more evident than within our wine industry. Our wine grapegrowers have endured years of difficult market conditions and oversupply of wine grapes, increasing input costs and, particularly, declining profitability.

Many growers are now considering what comes next, and it may mean diversifying into different crops, restructuring their businesses or, particularly, transitioning away from wine grapegrowing. Those decisions require capital, yet one of the constant messages I hear from growers is that accessing finance to undertake that transition is becoming increasingly difficult.

heading: Local Government (Transition Out of Administration) Amendment Bill (Bills) - 27/10/2026
subject: Local Government (Transition Out of Administration) Amendment Bill
parts: The Hon. R.A. SIMMS (16:18): I rise to indicate that the Greens will be supporting the Local Government (Transition Out of Administration) Amendment Bill, and I will outline our reasons for doing so in my remarks. I understand that in January 2019, the Coober Pedy council was placed into administration.

A history of mismanagement at the council, as demonstrated by the report of the former Ombudsman and later a report of the Auditor-General, was the basis of this decision. This report included serious findings of maladministration in the council's management of a power purchasing agreement for electricity generation for the town, as well as significant failings and deficiencies in the council's financial governance.

These matters were only intensified by the council's responsibility—and they are unique for any council in South Australia—for the delivery of essential water and energy services. They are also paired with a very considerable debt that the council accrued. I understand that the government has said that the council still has an energy debt of over $3.5 million and owes the Local Government Finance Authority $7.7 million in funds. The principal administrator has advised the government, in the strongest terms, of its concerns about the readiness of Coober Pedy council to return to an elected body at the next local government elections, given the significance and the complexity of the issues the administrators are working to solve.

heading: Local Government (Transition Out of Administration) Amendment Bill (Bills) - 27/10/2026
subject: Local Government (Transition Out of Administration) Amendment Bill
parts: I just make the point that some of the challenges faced by Coober Pedy are that, in these outback towns, they have a very large land mass and a very small rate base, so they do not have the sort of finances that city councils do that can employ experts in these fields to provide expert advice in making decisions regarding very complex issues. The very fact that there was maladministration found does not mean there was incompetence or whatever. The council is probably made up of very decent people who took on the role but just did not have the expertise or the money to help them make very good decisions at the time.

The Ombudsman found that the decision-making processes that led to the council signing the significant contract were so poor that he invited the then minister to consider exercising his power to recommend to the government that the council be declared defaulting. The Ombudsman's findings were supported by a lengthy examination of the council by the Auditor-General, finalised in late 2018, which identified significant failings and deficiency in the council's financial governance.

However, resolving the issues at Coober Pedy is significantly more difficult than it would be for other small regional councils because the council, uniquely amongst South Australian councils, is responsible for municipal and essential services delivery to the town. Under the Local Government Act 1999, a council in administration must return to an elected member body at the next periodical local government elections, which were in November 2022. However, it was readily apparent that it would not be responsible to require local elected members to manage the council at that point due to the significant issues that remain to be resolved in Coober Pedy.

parts: The Hon. K.J. MAHER (Deputy Premier, Minister for Aboriginal Affairs, Attorney-General, Minister for Industrial Relations, Minister for Arts, Special Minister of State): The Premier has advised:
No special investigation was undertaken by the Auditor-General in 2025-26.

Special investigations are uncommon and are only undertaken where there is a formal request or requirement under the provisions of the Public Finance and Audit Act 1987. The need for such investigations is driven by external circumstances and cannot be predicted in advance.

The Auditor-General does not maintain the annual audit program around the expectation that a special investigation will be undertaken. Rather, special investigations occur only when circumstances arise that warrant their use under the Public Finance and Audit Act 1987. As special investigations are infrequent and initiated in response to specific requests or statutory requirements, there have been a number of years in which no special investigation has been undertaken.

subject: Auditor-General's Report
parts: Mrs HURN: Starting with Part C: Agency Audit Outcomes, page 373, the Auditor-General's finding that the Department of State Development had not defined the frequency or extent of its monitoring of the security controls operated by the vendor SmartyGrants. The Auditor-General identified sensitive information held in the system, including bank details, financial performance data, business activity statements and debt information. In the second paragraph, can you just explain why the Department of State Development had not defined how often and to what extent it should assess and monitor the effectiveness of the vendor controls for the SmartyGrants system?

The Hon. C.J. PICTON: Thank you, and it is a pleasure to be with the member for Schubert for the fifth year in a row for Auditor-General's hearings, with slightly less money in the budget compared with previous years. I am advised that SmartyGrants is a cloud-based grants management system the department has used since 2022 to manage various grants programs under a software as a service arrangement. This system is also used across other state government entities. The system also records sensitive applicant information.

The Audit Office of South Australia recommended a security risk assessment for the department's use of the SmartyGrants system and determined the extent and frequency it should assess and monitor the vendor's security controls over the system. I have been advised that my department performed an initial security risk assessment of SmartyGrants when it procured the system, and completed a further security risk assessment of the system in June 2026, identifying controls and mitigation measures to consider.

Following the Auditor-General's advice and the recommendations in the June 2026 risk assessment, the department will consider relevant independent assurance reports, security certifications and other relevant security information and will conduct annual security risk assessments, taking into account changes to the service, emerging threats and current guidance. The department will also engage with the Office of the Chief Information Officer to explore using its whole-of-government supplier cybersecurity monitoring platform to support ongoing assurance over the SmartyGrants system.

The department is targeting 31 December 2026—the chief executive is going to be working on New Year's Eve to get that done, no doubt—to complete the initial review of the relevant independent assurance reports and security certifications and the engagement with the Office of the Chief Information Officer, with annual security risk assessments and assurance reviews to occur thereafter. I have been advised that no SmartyGrants cybersecurity breaches have been identified by the department and none have been reported to the department by the vendor.
Mrs HURN: It has been a platform since 2022, but how long has SmartyGrants operated without defined monitoring arrangements?

The Hon. C.J. PICTON: As I outlined in my lengthy answer, we have now put in place a number of different steps following the advice from the Auditor-General. That has happened this year, so it has been four years since the program was put in place in 2022. It is worth stressing, of course, that no cybersecurity breaches have been identified and none have been reported by the vendor, either.

Mrs HURN: Did the government undertake to speak proactively to any businesses that operate in SmartyGrants to determine that there was not any unauthorised access or disclosure of information in SmartyGrants?

The Hon. C.J. PICTON: The short answer is no. This is a risk that was identified by the Auditor-General that has been addressed. To our knowledge, there has not been any breach and there has not been any disclosure of information. If there had been, if we were aware of something, then that would be an entirely different situation in which it would be appropriate to reach out to businesses. This is a proactive measure that has been taken to address a potential risk. It is good to put in place these measures before anything has been identified as causing a problem. Therefore, it would not be standard practice to go out and communicate that with any business that might be part of the system.
Mrs HURN: The recommendation from the Auditor-General was that DSD assess the security risks for DSD's use of this SmartyGrants system. Who did that assessment?
Mrs HURN: What type of incident would spark the department into action to have an external audit of the SmartyGrants system?

The department has followed through in terms of the recommendation that has been put in place and has been liaising with the Office of the Chief Information Officer, as has also been recommended in the report. I am advised that that has been the appropriate outcome. We are getting into hypotheticals, but if there was a determination by the experts that it was not within their capability to be able to undertake that assessment—whether there was a higher risk, whether there was a more serious matter, or whether some of the issues that have not actually occurred, like actual cybersecurity breaches, had occurred—then they all might be factors that might indicate the need to obtain some external advice.

heading: Government Advertising Bill (Bills) - 14/10/2026
subject: Government Advertising Bill
parts: The Government Advertising Bill that I am introducing today imposes guidelines on government advertising and restricts government advertising in the lead-up to elections. I think this is a bill that actually reflects the will and the desire of the people of South Australia, people of our state who want to see the best possible standards in place when it comes to the spending of public money.

My bill will require the minister to establish guidelines for government advertising. Currently, there is no legislative requirement to do so and, as a result, the guidelines established by the government are voluntary. The bill would also ensure that MPs and ministers are prohibited from being featured in government ads, something that should be a no-brainer. It would ensure that advertising of bills currently before parliament would be prohibited along with the promotion of any political party figures. The Auditor-General would have new powers to investigate breaches and provide reports to parliament.

Critically, any government advertising of more than $10,000 in the lead-up to an election, from July of the year prior to the election, would be prohibited unless approved by the Auditor-General or the parliament itself on specified grounds. The Auditor-General would only be able to approve additional expenditure if it relates to public health, public safety, road and transport works, emergencies, material required to ensure that elections can be conducted, engagement of people in government services and attendance at events, tourism, sale of property or courses of tertiary institutions.

I think it is very fair that the Auditor-General should cast an eye over any advertising in the lead-up to an election to ensure that it is appropriate. I also note my bill ensures that social media advertising is captured in these provisions and it improves transparency overall. Critically, the bill also contains a provision that requires the government to disclose its election commitment tracking annually. This ensures that the work of the Premier's Delivery Unit is appropriately disclosed to Parliament.

This bill will not be new to many members of this parliament. Indeed, back in 2021, the then Malinauskas government introduced some changes to the Electoral Act. At that time, the Greens moved an amendment to ensure that in the lead-up to elections no government advertising would be able to proceed without the approval of the Auditor-General or both houses of parliament. That amendment was supported by the Labor opposition. Indeed, the amendment was based on a private member's bill that had been introduced into the other place by the then shadow treasurer, Stephen Mullighan.

The Labor Party were very enthusiastic about it when they were in opposition—very enthusiastic indeed when they were in opposition. But what happened when they got into government? Surprise, surprise! Despite their enthusiasm for this when they were in opposition, their enthusiasm for transparency when they were in opposition, once they got into government, suddenly they went really cold on the idea. Members will recall that I introduced a very similar bill into the previous parliament. It was supported by all other political parties in this place except for—

Might I also say that my fear is that this is just a drop in the ocean, because we also know that this does not include spending that is subject to commercial-in-confidence arrangements. How much money have South Australian taxpayers forked out for LIV Golf? The Malinauskas government, over a year ago now, announced with great fanfare—the Hon. Sarah Game was there along with the Hon. Connie Bonaros—that we were going to be investing a huge amount of taxpayer funds into redeveloping the North Adelaide Golf Course to keep LIV Golf here. We know now that has been a colossal flop; it is going bankrupt.

We know from today's discussion that the government have not even done their due diligence around looking at a business case or getting any cost-benefit analysis done, and the Auditor-General has made some statements reflecting their lack of due diligence. How much government funds have been spent on promoting LIV Golf? South Australian taxpayers have a right to know. It is public money, and when we are talking about public money, there should be maximum transparency.

This is the problem when it comes to this Labor government's approach to these matters. They do not like transparency, they do not like to answer questions. Indeed, question time should be changed to answer time because they are more interested in just backslapping and telling us how great they are, but when it comes to a question from the crossbench or the opposition, they are not willing to answer it. Really, this government has a transparency problem and this bill seeks to shine a light on how they are spending taxpayer funds. It seeks to ensure that there is more transparency and restrictions around government advertising, and I think it accords with community expectations.

parts: At the retail level, you had people owing up to $8,000, $9,000 or $10,000 a year. There are regulatory requirements when it comes to electricity providers, like hardship provisions and the rest of it. That is fine when you are talking about grid-connected people and retailers who have thousands and thousands of customers, so that hardship provision can be spread across a big population base. That was just not possible in Coober Pedy. As someone who did represent the community at one stage, it was my view, and it was my view very early on in the piece, that Coober Pedy council had to be shrunk down to basic municipal services.

Some time before the Ombudsman and the Auditor-General flagged serious maladministration—it could have been six months, seven months before—the ABC interviewed me. I was asked point-blank whether the Coober Pedy council should be sacked. My response was just straightforward. I said, 'Yes, it should be sacked.' Two weeks later, I was in Coober Pedy. The council asked me to go to see them, so I went and met with the whole of the council. It was a bit icy to start with. It was a long meeting; it probably went for about two hours. It was a worthwhile meeting.

It is not that I lacked sympathy for the council, or certainly for some of the people on the council, because the challenges that they faced were significant. For a remote community trying to attract professionals as CEOs, as people who do the finance and for other senior positions, it is difficult. They had revolving-door CEOs. They had revolving-door finance officers. They had revolving-door mayors. There were some real challenges in that community. You would have to say that some of the CEOs and some of the finance officers left a lot to be desired.

We ended up with a situation, and it is a complex situation, whereby the Auditor-General and the Ombudsman flagged serious maladministration. I was not pre-empting any decision; I was just expressing an opinion in those months beforehand. You cannot just sack a council. There has to be, understandably, a process. It was during the term of the Marshall government that Stephan Knoll as the minister at the time decided that, yes, the thing to do was to put the council into administration. That had my full support.

This has dragged on since those days, and we are still faced with the basics. We have indicated that SA Water, and I have advocated for this for a long time, take over the whole water supply and distribution system in Coober Pedy. I also believe retail and distribution needs to be outsourced. In saying that, I just want to pay credit to the workers on the ground in Coober Pedy who kept those systems going through all those management changes, all that having to do things on the smell of an oily rag. It was a credit to that workforce, what they were able to do under very difficult circumstances.

heading: Rural Industry Adjustment and Development (Loan Interest) Amendment Bill (Bills) - 02/09/2026
subject: Rural Industry Adjustment and Development (Loan Interest) Amendment Bill
speakerRaw: The Hon. N.J. CENTOFANTI (Leader of the Opposition) (16:47)
parts: The fund was established from accumulated state funds arising from earlier commonwealth-state rural assistance arrangements and was deliberately designed to give South Australia greater capacity to determine how those funds could be used to assist our agricultural industries. Importantly, the original intent was not limited to emergency relief. When the legislation was introduced, there was a clear focus on supporting industries and regions where structural adjustment and redevelopment were required. There was also recognition that producers seeking that adjustment or redevelopment may not always be able to obtain the necessary finance through normal commercial credit sources. Forty-one years later that principle remains just as relevant.

Today, according to the Auditor-General, approximately $28.4 million remains in the Rural Industry Adjustment and Development Fund. At the same time, parts of South Australian primary industries are experiencing significant structural pressures. Nowhere is that more evident than in our wine industry currently. Our wine grapegrowers have endured years of difficult market conditions and oversupply of wine and grapes, increasing input costs and declining profitability. Many growers are now considering what comes next. It may mean diversifying into different crops, restructuring their business or transitioning land away from wine grapes altogether, and those decisions require capital. Yet, one of the consistent messages I hear from growers is that accessing finance to undertake that transition is increasingly difficult.

Commercial banks are understandably assessing risk against the current state of the industry. That means growers who may have viable plans for their future can find themselves unable to access the finance required to actually implement those plans. That is where government can play a constructive role. This is not about writing blank cheques, it is not about propping up businesses that have no prospect of being viable and it is not about replacing commercial banks. It is about providing a hand up, not a handout, to viable primary producers who have a credible pathway forward but cannot reasonably obtain the finance they need on commercial terms.

heading: Public Finance Transparency Bill (Bills) - 17/06/2026

parts: By 2030, we will be paying $3.5 billion each and every year in interest payments alone. heading: Supply Bill 2026 (Bills) - 16/06/2026
subject: Supply Bill 2026
parts: The $1.4 billion figure only reaches $1.4 billion by counting the year that is almost over. Strip that out from the current year and look at the four years ahead. The budget is actually around $1.18 billion of surplus. The operating surplus that the Treasurer is boasting about ultimately is an accounting measure. It is not the cash position of the state and the cash position, that net lending figure, the measure of whether the state is actually living within its means or not, is in deficit every single year of the forward estimates: a deficit of $2.1 billion this year, $3.3 billion the next and nearly $4 billion the year after that.

In total, across the forward estimates, this government will borrow around $15 billion in cash. Let me put it as plainly as I can: a surplus where you have to borrow $15 billion to deliver is not a surplus at all. How did we get here? Through a complete and sustained failure to control spending. In 2025-26 alone, the government overspent its own budget by $1.2 billion—not a rounding error, but $1.2 billion. This was not a failure of one rogue department. Of 28 agencies of government, 27 of them went over their budget. All but a single agency blew its budget and, surprise, surprise, that was the Auditor-General, whose job is, I think, to make sure people stay on the right track in terms of their spending, which 27 out of 28 departmental agencies in this state have not done.

When every single agency blew its budget, you might say, 'Okay, that's just a bit of a mishap for this financial year.' But no, let us look at the last four years. Every single year departments have blown their budgets to the tune of $6 billion—$6 billion that has not gone anywhere, but has been blown. The government will tell us that it is exercising restraint. The centrepiece of that restraint is their partial hiring freeze, a measure the Treasurer says will save around $120 million a year and reduce non-frontline positions by about 1,000. If you set that against the $1.2 billion that this government has overspent in its own budget this year alone, the scale of the problem is laid bare.

heading: Eastick, Hon. Dr B.C. (Condolence) - 20/05/2026
subject: Eastick, Hon. Dr B.C.
parts: Not only was Bruce a fierce presence for his electorate, but he was also a really persistent advocate for road safety, calling in this house for random breath testing, tougher drink-driving legislation, and improved seatbelt design at a time when those causes were far from settled policy. He pushed for car-mounted police video cameras to catch road offenders, a proposal that was genuinely ahead of its time. He raised concerns about police staffing, morale and resources and held the government to account on police working conditions.

On industrial matters, he challenged compulsory unionism and called for secret ballots for trade unions as a matter of democratic principle. On economic management, he called for the abolition of the South Australian petrol tax and questioned the accuracy of Auditor-General reporting on public sector finances—brave man.

He also identified and raised in the chamber a significant problem with the state electoral rolls, demonstrating that hundreds of voters in the District of Light were in fact enrolled in the wrong electorate. These were not narrow concerns, they were interventions of a man who used his time in this place to press for practical improvements in the lives of South Australians. Just 20 months after entering this house, his colleagues elected him as Leader of the Opposition in March 1972. He approached that role with the same directness that he brought to everything before it. Writing at the time, political reporter, Michael Cudmore, observed that Bruce would not fail through any lack of personal effort and determination and described him as a truly humane man with basic integrity, a capacity for hard work and an almost bewildering attention to detail.

Mr TELFER (Flinders) (15:08): Yesterday a very interesting document was tabled in parliament looking at the Auditor-General's Report, No. 9 of 2025, State Finances—Insights on the 2025-26 Budget. It is not as big a document as some of the ones that get tabled here in this place but it is one that is full of content that South Australians would rightly be really concerned about.

I want to highlight a few of these aspects just to shine a light on the fact that the Auditor-General has laid bare some of those financial concerns that Labor are blindly taking our state into. To start, looking at net debt in particular, the Auditor-General talks about net debt and makes the comment that it continues to rise and is forecast to reach $48.5 billion by 2029—$48.5 billion. That number is eye-watering. That number is one which South Australians struggle to comprehend. That number is exponentially worse than any level of debt that South Australia has ever been in, even when taking into consideration the equivalent dollars that we are facing.

Some of the commentary that the Auditor-General has put in the report should make South Australians stand up and take notice. Net debt is projected to rise to 26 per cent of gross state product by 2029. The Auditor-General talks about net debt as a proportion of GSP being a common measure used by state governments to assess financial sustainability. It gives the advice that the commonwealth Parliamentary Budget Office considers a sustainable fiscal position to be one where net debt as a proportion of GSP is expected to be stable or to trend down over the long term. If you look at the graph that is within this report, South Australia sadly is in a higher trajectory when it comes to net debt to GSP. Things are only getting worse under this Labor government, and some of the commentary that has been provided by the Auditor-General is truly concerning.

Net debt in itself is not a bad thing, but when it is growing at a faster rate than revenue it should be ringing alarm bells for the Treasurer and for the Premier, because this is the situation that Labor is putting us in. If net debt is rising quicker than the revenue, we are only getting ourselves further and further into debt.

As I said, debt in itself is not a bad thing if it is used wisely, but some of the commentary that the Auditor-General makes is also about the restriction that it puts on the opportunities for future growth for our state. Not just the debt burden but the interest burden that is being faced by South Australia because of this debt is truly astronomical. The rising interest expense may constrain the state's fiscal capacity. Basically, the amount that we are paying in interest is going to significantly limit the amount of money that governments in the future are going to be able to put as investments into the community to pay for the things that are really important.

Interest expense as a total proportion of total revenue is expected to reach 8.3 per cent in 2028-29. Once again, it is a number that some people struggle to get their head around. It is up from 5.4 per cent in 2024-25, and it is going to be payments, repayments and interest payments of nearly $7 million a day—$7 million a day, each and every day, 365 days a year, and that number is only growing. Imagine what could be paid for with an extra $7 million. This is debt burden that state Labor is putting us under without any sort of management plan in place.

When the Premier was opposition leader he crowed about the importance of debt management. He called on the previous government to have a debt management plan in place. He said that that is exactly what they would do in government. Well, we are still waiting. We are nearly four years in and there is no plan to manage the debt that Labor is taking us down. Do not forget that that debt number is exponentially higher than under the previous government—record levels of debt, nearly $48.5 billion. What does Labor do about it? Just hope that it all goes away.

Some of the commentary from the Auditor-General about this is particularly worrying. It is not just about debt, it is also about budget management. The Auditor-General, in making commentary around the importance of budget management, states that robust performance monitoring is required for existing budget programs to inform decision-making. What does that mean? It means that ministers and departments should be conscientious in the way that they spend taxpayers' money. They should be managing their budget in a responsible way.

As highlighted, this was a contract signed off under the previous government, one that has left us, I guess, in a situation where it is difficult to dig up. This is a contract we have inherited that is not fit for purpose. Needless to say, we do continue to work with Ventia to ensure that we can have better outcomes.

Just to highlight some of the things that are highlighted in the Auditor-General's Report, I think on the same page—page 234 from memory, or maybe further—are the things that the contractor is seen as not achieving. Subcontractors are engaged who charge above the maximum trade ceiling rates established under the contract, with agencies charged at rates higher than those allowed for some work; failure to meet KPI targets for response and restoration times for breakdown jobs; and maintenance work often not completed within the required timeframes.

I understand the department has been working with Ventia to work through this contract. Yes, there are improvements that can be done on both sides, and that is acknowledged. That is something that both the department and Ventia are working towards.

Internal and external assurances and audit activities of the systems, processes and work orders have been performed. These activities are being used to further update the information, the risk register and audit, and the insurance plans and contract management plans. Steps have continuously been put in place to make sure that Ventia can meet their contractual requirements here. The conversations do continue, and they have had to continue regularly to try to make sure we can have an outcome that we can all hope is a positive one, because at the end of the day it is our facilities in our communities that are missing out.

There are definitely steps being put in place—that is acknowledged I think also in the Auditor-General's Report of what actions they are taking. That is highlighted within the report and recorded in there as well.

BOURKE: I understand from the advice given that every effort is being made and we are now at the point of having to provide breach notices where that is required, but as highlighted before this is not a matter of set and forget. I think that is also highlighted in the Auditor-General's Report on page 234, the opening line acknowledging that DIT has been working continuously to improve Ventia's service delivery.

Yes, it is acknowledged that there is work that has been undertaken and it is acknowledged that work still needs to be undertaken. We appreciate that and it has been addressed within the report findings, but at the end of the day this is a contract that we inherited, it is not fit for purpose and we are now having to find ways to manage a contract that was not built to be able to support the services that are needed in South Australia.

The Hon. N.D. CHAMPION: Yes.

parts: The Hon. K.A. HILDYARD: Thank you to the member for the question. As the Auditor-General points out, we are seeing a significant reduction in the growth of the number of children and young people coming into care. Those levers that we have used to assist with that result include, as the Auditor-General also refers to, our successful Finding Families program, our successful Additionally Approved Carer Program and our investment in family group conferencing. Expenditure is directed to each of those programs and also to our reunification efforts. Those programs are delivering results that are directly showing that reduction in terms of the growth of the number of children and young people coming into care.

What we also find, though, is that, whilst we are reducing the number of children and young people coming into care, the children and young people who are in care have increasingly a range of complexities that we need to respond to. That means that we need to contract particular services to ensure that the complex needs of particular children and young people are absolutely met.
Mr TEAGUE: I am not sure that is an answer. The Auditor-General has found that they were incorrect payments, so is the minister's answer that that all just gets left?

The Hon. R.K. PEARCE: This is another area that I am pleased to share that we have had significant improvements in. Originally, it was looking at about 68 fleet assets. That is down now to approximately 30. A lot of those are trailers that are being decommissioned and we have been putting others in place that are to a higher standard.

The Hon. R.K. PEARCE: Thank you very much for the question. I understand that from time to time there can be minor incidents that occur that are not attributable to the condition of the trailer. As you can understand, being on the road sometimes that can occur. There was a minor incident that happened, I understand, on Kangaroo Island. It was minor in the sense that no injuries occurred in that particular case.

Mr WHETSTONE: In the last four Auditor-General Reports, he has reported that the emergency service sector should develop strategic asset management plans. In this year's report, he found that limited progress had been made on these plans. What is the current status of those plans and when are they expected to be completed?

The Hon. R.K. PEARCE: In regard to the SES, a detailed review and data analysis has been underway in terms of the fleets that we have in place and we continue to update those figures. We do have an ongoing audit and targeted action plan to help address the gaps as we see fit as well and there are also enhancements planned to Emerald, which is the SES data recording system, which will include automated notifications for servicing and also maintenance deadlines, reminders to ensure timely documentation, and also the escalation points to address overdue or missing records. Essentially, they aim to further improve the document recording and data analysis capabilities that we see.
